A full technical account of the platform as it stands on 17 August 2026 — the week's changes and the reasoning behind them, the unit economics measured against live provider prices, the metrics worth watching, and the sequenced work that follows.

Headline: the code is live and both media paths are now proven.

Commit e831e05 is on main, pushed, and auto-deployed by Hostinger — production is serving this week's work. Every required readiness check is green, including private media storage, which was the blocker. A video has since been generated, saved and played back from a real account, and the image path has been verified end to end with a real 1.7MB generated file. The central feature of the product is repaired in fact, not in theory.

02What changed this week, and why

Six decisions and one incident, each recorded in DECISIONS.md with its reasoning. Presented as before and after, because in every case the old behaviour was defensible-looking and wrong.

1 · Private media storage was never configured in production
Was Renders completed at the provider and were then lost. The studio showed “Rendering…” forever because a failed save was treated as a passing fault and retried indefinitely. Images appeared to work because they fall back to a temporary base64 copy that is never stored. The real error existed only in host logs.
Now MediaStorageNotConfiguredError is typed and terminal: the job fails, the full credit hold is refunded, and the person is told. Delivery that is still failing 30 minutes after the provider finished is also terminal. The real reason is written to the job row. /api/ready gained a required media_storage check.
2 · Video had one price when it should have had two
Was Every render silently used the expensive engine at 19 credits. A cheaper engine existed in the catalogue and was never offered. The credit floor of 12 meant even a cheap clip was charged nearly the full rate, so choosing it would have bought the customer little.
Now The quote drives the hold. Floor cut 12 → 6, ceiling raised 20 → 24. A draft clip costs about 7 credits against 19 for the best engine — roughly a third — and the ceiling change lifts engine headroom from 7% to 23%.
3 · The landing page promised what a visitor could not have
Was Three of four hero starters and four of six outcome cards routed to agent or studio, which require an account. A signed-out visitor clicking “Take the first step” received POST /api/agent → 401 and an error card with a UUID as their first experience. The page said “Start free, no card”.
Now Free chat paths lead; gated starters carry a “Free account” badge before they are clicked. An empty click runs a real question on the free path instead of opening another empty box. Pre-written prompt stems no longer submit as goals.
4 · Eight labels pointed at one destination
Was “Take the first step”, “Start with your goal”, “Start with a goal”, “Start now”, “Try it now”, “Open AI360”, “Open workspace”, “Continue as a guest” — all to /app, each written by hand. The hero submitted immediately while outcome cards only prefilled, with no rule distinguishing them.
Now One StartCta owns label, destination and send-or-prefill. “Start free” signed out, “Open workspace” signed in. The rule is explicit: what the person typed runs; what we pre-wrote waits.
5 · Naming and pilot language
Was Nav said “Plans”, the URL was /pricing, metadata said both. Paid surfaces described a private trial — “One-month pilot access”, “Join the Everyday pilot” — while charging real money. The terms claimed prices were “a pilot proposal until checkout is activated” and that top-ups were not sold. Both were untrue.
Now The page is Pricing; the products on it are plans. Pilot language is gone from every charged surface while the real constraints stay stated: one month per payment, no automatic renewal, no annual billing yet.
6 · The type scale was a quarter too small
Was Body copy 15px. On the landing page at 1280px, 76 of 166 text elements sat below 12px, the smallest at 7px. Across all stylesheets, 432 of 883 font-size declarations were under 12px. The product looked better at 125% browser zoom because zoom was correcting a real defect.
Now Every font-size scaled on a curve, heaviest at the small end, 12px floor. Body is 17px; nothing is under 12px; longest line fell from 90 to 72 characters. Spacing untouched, so no layout could reflow. Verified at 375, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1440px.

A seventh change nobody asked for: cost telemetry

The video status endpoint recorded the provider's full job cost on every poll. 150 polls of three renders were recorded as $47.80 of spend against roughly $0.96 of real cost — a fifty-fold overstatement, in exactly the number a pricing decision would be made from. Now only a terminal status carries the cost, and only once.

The ceiling is now per second, not per render. A flat cap could not describe an engine that charges by the second: at 24 credits it refused an eight-second clip outright, and it also made the premium engine unsellable, so “Best” silently resolved to the same engine as “Better” — a tier that existed in name only. At 12 credits a second the four-second cap is unchanged at 48, every length from 4 to 8 seconds is priced proportionally, and the promise that nothing costs more than the person saw is carried by the quote they accept rather than by the cap. Re-run scripts/audit-media-pricing.mjs whenever the provider moves prices.

Real spend to date

Corrected for the polling over-count, total provider spend across the entire life of the product is approximately $1.40 — about GH₵21. The recorded figure of $48.22 was an artefact. This matters because it is the denominator for every efficiency claim.

04Technical decisions and the guardrails they set

Each of these is now written into DECISIONS.md as a rule, not a fix, because the same class of failure recurred three times this week.

Storage is a readiness requirement

If a deliverable only exists once it is stored, storage is a required health check — not an assumption. Production reported "ready" for two days while unable to keep a single file.

A retry loop must classify its faults

Transient and permanent failures need different handling. An unset environment variable cannot be retried into working, and treating it as transient produced an infinite spinner.

No surface holds its own copy of a price

Four separate drifts this week: the pricing page, the assistant's product knowledge, the chat daily caps, and the credit guide. Every published number is now derived from the module that charges.

A call to action is a promise about the next screen

"Take the first step" is only honest when a first step follows. Gating and copy are one decision, never two.

Typed errors over string matching

MediaStorageNotConfiguredError lets callers branch on cause rather than parsing messages, which is what allowed a permanent fault to be classified correctly.

Settlement must never break delivery

An unguarded settleReservation in the status path could turn every later poll into a 500 the client retried forever — so a delivered clip could still read as "Rendering…".

Diagnostic tooling added

The storage incident took a database query, a provider replay and a bucket write probe to isolate. That work is now one command each, so the next occurrence is minutes rather than hours.

ScriptAnswers
diagnose-video-jobs.mjsDurable jobs, credit holds, live provider status, and a bucket write probe
diagnose-video-delivery.mjsReplays download → upload → rows against a stuck job; rolls back by default, --commit to deliver
diagnose-media-storage.mjsWhat production itself recorded when storage failed
verify-media-roundtrip.mjsProves image and video can be stored and read back, then cleans up

07Next steps, sequenced

Ordered by what unblocks the most. The first block is measured in minutes and settles the question the whole product rests on.

Today · prove the repair

1. Generate one image in production. Confirm a row appears in lab_assets and the file opens from the gallery.

2. Generate one 4-second draft video. Confirm it persists, the credits settle to the measured cost, and the clip plays.

3. Deliver the stuck clip with node scripts/diagnose-video-delivery.mjs --commit, then settle the 38 credits owed on the two undelivered renders.

4. Look at the new type scale at 100% zoom on a phone and a laptop, and confirm it matches what you saw at 125%.

This week

  1. Turn on transactional email. Complete the domain verification step and set EMAIL_ENABLED=true, so a paying customer gets a receipt without one being sent by hand.
  2. Generate one image through the signed-in studio. The provider, guards, upload, asset row and read-back are each verified with a real 1.7MB image; the only untested link is the authenticated route wrapper, which video has already exercised live.
  3. Add the delivery-gap query to a daily cron. Terminal jobs without a stored output, and reservations settled without delivery. This is the check that would have caught the storage failure in an hour rather than two days.
  4. Provision the Axiom dataset so logs are searchable rather than only alertable through Sentry.
  5. Rewrite the roadmap against what is actually true, with the phase drift resolved.

Next two to four weeks

  1. Carry the goal through sign-up. A visitor who picks a gated starter should sign up and have their goal run immediately, rather than losing it at the wall.
  2. Resolve the duplicate render. Roughly a quarter of every marketing page's HTML is a hidden second copy, with duplicate DOM ids, on connections where weight is expensive.
  3. The spacing pass. The other half of the 125% effect. Higher layout risk than the type change, so it needs the same width-by-width verification.
  4. Instrument return visits so retention becomes measurable rather than assumed.
  5. Get the first agent run from a real user — offer a guided agent task in onboarding and watch what happens.

Beyond, gated on evidence

  1. Annual billing, only after repeat payments, reversals and refunds are proven end to end.
  2. Second media provider for engine redundancy and pricing leverage.
  3. Team workspaces, currently flag-disabled, once single-user retention is real.
  4. The moat work: local context, language coverage and product self-knowledge are the parts a global competitor cannot copy cheaply.

08How this fits AI360 and AIC

This codebase — formerly “AI360 Lab”, now simply AI360 — carries four institutional jobs at once. They are compatible, but they are measured differently, and confusing them is how a product ends up optimising for the wrong thing.

1 · A commercial product

Revenue from Ghanaian individuals and businesses, at 70–79% gross margin per credit. Proven once, with GH₵125 collected end to end. The economics work; the volume does not exist yet.

Measured by: paying customers, margin per credit, cost per active account.

2 · Digital inclusion and capability

Frontier AI made usable for students, traders, NGOs and public servants — in plain language, on a phone, on an interrupted connection, priced in cedis with Mobile Money. Most of the product's hardest engineering serves this rather than any feature list.

Measured by: completed real outcomes, not sign-ups.

3 · Proof of AIC's capability

A live production system with credit metering, payment reconciliation, durable job recovery, error tracking and an incident discipline. This week it detected, diagnosed and fixed a silent revenue-affecting fault from its own records. That is the evidence that AIC can operate software, not only build it.

Measured by: uptime, incident quality, decision record.

4 · An investment and partnership case

The architecture reads as fundable: honest unit economics, enforced spend ceilings, no silent overage, provider independence, and a written record of every trade-off. What is missing is traction, and traction is now the binding constraint rather than capability.

Measured by: growth rate, retention, unit economics at scale.

The strategic read

The build risk is largely behind us; the demand risk is entirely ahead. The platform can take money, meter work, recover from failure and tell the truth about cost. It has eleven accounts, one payment and no delivered creative output. Every remaining question is about whether people in Accra will use and pay for this — and none of them can be answered by more engineering.

Which argues for a deliberate order: prove media delivery today, put the product in front of a first cohort of twenty real users this month, and let what they actually do decide the next phase of the roadmap rather than the plan written before they existed.
